subject: ventures/world-clock-widget
professional: a mobile engineer who ships WidgetKit apps, with a solar-position/almanac practitioner (a navigator or astronomy-software maintainer) checking the sunrise/sunset numbers and a time-zone/ICU specialist checking DST and day-boundary handling. First checks: sunrise/sunset against the USNO/NOAA tables, the local-day boundary, DST-transition days, and whether the widget's minute entries flip on the minute.

evidence.correctness: Swift is not installed in this container (`which swift` empty), so no Swift code ran. That caps this at 2 and means the Swift suite (Tests/WorldClockCoreTests, 4 files) was not executed by me. What I ran: site/solar.mjs, the line-for-line JS port of SolarCalculator.swift (I diffed the steps by reading: same constants 0.9856, 3.289, 1.916, 0.020, 282.634, 0.91764, 0.39782, 90.83, 0.06571, 6.622 and the same +/-1 day nudge). I dumped sunrise/sunset for all 40 catalog cities on 4 dates (2026-03-20, 03-29, 06-21, 12-21; 160 city-dates x 2 events) and recomputed each independently in Python with zoneinfo and the NOAA/Meeus solar-position equations (a source the author did not write, different algorithm, zenith 90.833). Result: 0 of 160 differ by more than 3 minutes; the worst are Reykjavik at the March equinox (+1.3 min sunrise, -0.9 min sunset), London +0.9/-0.5, Tokyo +0.6/-0.2 and LA +0.6/-0.2; on 21 June London, Tokyo, LA and Sydney are within 0.2 min. The local-calendar-day nudge returned the right local date in every case, including 29 March (a DST-change week for London, Sydney). So the algorithm as ported is right to about a minute, which matches the README claim. Not verified: the Swift binary itself, DateFormatter output, the day-offset label across a DST boundary (all Swift tests use 1 January).
evidence.completeness: README claims checked: (1) WorldClockCore with City model, 40-city catalog, solar math, formatting, shared store: all present in Sources/WorldClockCore, 40 City(...) entries, matching the '~40' claim; (2) 'catalog in sync with the site' (CITIES): site test passes; (3) widget small/medium/large/XL plus lock-screen rectangular/inline with per-widget city choice by App Intents: files exist (WorldClockWidgetViews.swift 249 lines, SelectCitiesIntent, CityOption with all 40 cases) but unbuilt and unrun here, and README itself says App and Widget are 'unverified'; (4) one timeline entry per minute for an hour: implemented at CityTimelineProvider.swift:24-30; (5) Linux CI for WorldClockCore via Package.swift: manifest and workflow exist, I could not check a green run; (6) 'Mac (Designed for iPad)': project.yml-only claim, not built. The browser surface in site/ (the only one that reaches users) works: 53 node tests pass, three pages present. Every iOS surface is blocked-on-owner (VENTURE.yaml), so end-to-end completeness for the app is not demonstrated. README does not mention the web tool at all besides the live-page link.
evidence.verification: Ran `cd ventures/world-clock-widget/site && node --test *.test.mjs`: 53 pass, 0 fail. The Swift suites (`swift test`) could not run: no swift. Mutations seeded in site/solar.mjs (the port the tests cover), each reverted with `git checkout -- solar.mjs`, `git status` clean afterward: (a) OFFICIAL_ZENITH 90.83 -> 90.0 shifts every sunrise/sunset by several minutes and 53/53 STILL PASS, so a real constant error survived; (b) the 0.06571*approxTime term scaled by 1.3: 3 tests failed (caught); (c) removing the +/-1 day nudge: 5 failed (caught). The survivor is explained by the London reference test, which allows +/-20 minutes (solar.test.mjs:73-74; the Swift twin allows 20 min at SolarCalculatorTests.swift) while the README and page claim 'about a minute'. Nothing in either suite pins a sunrise to the stated accuracy, and nothing tests a DST-transition day or the Swift day-offset label away from 1 January. The Swift mutant itself was not run.
evidence.craft: Read in full: SolarCalculator.swift, CityClockSnapshot.swift, CityTimeFormatting.swift, CityCatalog.swift, CityTimelineProvider.swift, Package.swift, and site/solar.mjs lines 1-260. Clean: small files, a lock-guarded DateFormatter cache keyed by locale/zone/styles, comments saying why, the polar guard returns nil rather than NaN, CityOption raw values equal City.id. Defects: (1) CityTimelineProvider builds entries at `now + n minutes` with no rounding to the minute, so if the timeline is fetched at 12:00:40 the displayed minute changes at :40 past, up to 59 s late for a clock whose purpose is the time; (2) CityTimelineProvider.swift:23 uses Calendar(identifier: .gregorian) with the device zone only for date arithmetic, harmless but unneeded; (3) the solar core is duplicated in Swift and JS by design (a copied engine, kept in step by a length/id test, not by shared vectors); (4) isDaytime defaults to true when sunrise is nil, which is wrong for polar night (unreachable with this catalog); (5) CityCatalog 'Reykjavik' at 64 degrees is the practical limit and nothing checks the sunrise for days near the summer solstice in Swift.
evidence.claims: Checked: 'accurate to roughly a minute outside the polar circles' (README, page, solar.mjs): backed by my 160-case recomputation (worst 1.3 min) but NOT by any test in the repo (tests allow 20 min). 'No network calls / no API key': grep of site/ and Sources/WorldClockCore finds none, and page.test.mjs asserts it. Page disclaimer present ('free and as-is, without warranty', 'estimates... not advice'). Unbacked or inconsistent: VENTURE.yaml says the iOS code is 'complete and tested' while README says the App and Widget targets are 'unverified' and no Xcode was ever available; the Swift core tests were last stated to run on Linux CI but I could not confirm a green run. README 'Tests' section lists only the xcodebuild command and omits the 53 site tests and CityTimeFormattingTests/CityCatalogTests. llms.txt links to the old duncan-haywood.github.io address, which hosting docs say now only redirects to https://marisstella.app/. VENTURE.yaml hypotheses are all 'untested', which is stated honestly.
evidence.fitness: Job: a person with colleagues or family abroad checks local time, whether they are awake, and sunrise/sunset. The web tool covers that job today with 40 fixed cities, no account, no network. The iPhone widget, the stated primary product, cannot reach anyone (no Apple developer account, `blocked-on-owner`) and has never been built or seen on a simulator. Fixed 40-city list means a user in e.g. Lisbon, Perth or Kathmandu cannot add their own city (acknowledged limitation). The user with a city the catalog lacks, or on a lock screen, is not served.
evidence.domain: Method compared against: USNO Almanac for Computers 1990 sunrise/sunset algorithm (the one named) and NOAA's Meeus-based calculator. The choice is the standard one for a clock widget, the 90.83 degree zenith includes refraction and the solar semi-diameter, the quadrant handling for right ascension is correct, and my independent NOAA recompute agrees within 1.3 minutes everywhere tested. Departures a practitioner would note: city-centre coordinates and no elevation (disclosed); uses IANA time zones via system tzdata, which is the right source; zoneinfo and DST behaviour is delegated to the platform; the almanac method degrades near the polar circles (Reykjavik worst case in the sample) and the project says so; no twilight times, which an astronomer would expect but the product does not claim.

defects.what: Test tolerance (+/-20 min) is 20x looser than the 'about a minute' accuracy claim; changing the zenith constant from 90.83 to 90.0 passes all 53 site tests, and the Swift suite uses the same tolerance.
Widget timeline entries are generated at now + n minutes with no alignment to the minute boundary, so the displayed minute can change up to 59 s late.
VENTURE.yaml says the iOS code is 'complete and tested' but the README says the App and Widget are unverified and never built; the Swift tests are not shown to run anywhere I could check.
llms.txt links to the old github.io address which now only redirects to marisstella.app.
README Tests section omits the 53 site tests and two of the four Swift test files.
isDaytime returns true when sunrise/sunset are nil, which is wrong for polar night (unreachable with the shipped catalog).

verdict: The part that reaches users, the browser tool, is correct: its solar maths agrees with an independent NOAA/Meeus implementation within 1.3 minutes on 160 city-dates, it honours the local-day boundary, and its claims and disclaimer are backed. The thing the venture is named for, the iOS widget, was not executed by anyone I can verify: swift is not installed here, so none of the Swift or its 4 test files ran, and the app and widget targets have never been built. Its tests would not catch a several-minute constant error (the zenith mutant survived a 20-minute tolerance), and nothing covers DST days or the Swift day-offset label away from 1 January. The code is tidy but the timeline entries are not minute-aligned, and VENTURE.yaml overstates 'complete and tested'. It does not meet the bar (verification and claims are 2) and is not finished (completeness 2).
